name: Yellowish cinnamon
lede: Yellowish cinnamon is ColorHub's English name for Akashirotsurubami, a Japanese traditional color meaning "sawtooth oak," a near relative of [[yellowish-camel]]'s "white oak."

sections.title: Sawtooth oak
sections.body:
赤白橡 (Akashirotsurubami) means sawtooth oak, pairing the modifier "reddish" with the same shirotsurubami root as Yellowish camel, and landing a shade warmer and pinker [1]. Our sources give no precise date for the name's origin, as is typical of Japanese traditional colors here [1].

Its nearest look-alike is [[apricot-buff]], 2.7 units away, almost the same; [[atomic-tangerine]] at 3.7 reads more vivid, and [[dark-salmon]] at 3.9 duller [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The color appears in 0.35 percent of 23,781 paintings, 84 of them as photographed, more common than 50 percent of the names we track [3]. It peaks in the 1500s, found in 0.6 percent of the 2,231 paintings we have from then, 13 of them, 2.3 times the expected rate [3]. Inside a painting it plays an accent 77 percent of the time [3]. The earliest dated match is a panel from 1150, though the archive's early centuries are thin enough that this is a floor, not a first [3].

questions.q: What does Akashirotsurubami, the Japanese name behind Yellowish cinnamon, mean?
True or false: Yellowish cinnamon and Yellowish camel share the same tsurubami (oak) root in Japanese.

openers: Yellowish cinnamon shares its Japanese root word with Yellowish camel: tsurubami, oak.
